turns.en: Kari wrote this blog post like issue tracking is dead. So how do you explain to your customers that hey, our entire business was issue tracking before and now our CEO just wrote this blog post?
turns.zh: Kari 写了这篇博客文章，说问题跟踪已死。那么你怎么向客户解释，嘿，我们整个业务以前就是问题跟踪，现在我们的 CEO 刚写了这篇博客文章？

turns.en: The great thing about our business is that we're not so big as to kill ourselves, right? It's probably really hard if you're Google to kill the search business, right? And put an AI box at the top of every search result and maybe no one's going to look at the ads, right? So your entire business is upended. And yes, the unit of the issue still exists, but we probably shouldn't have a world where people are manually tracking work. So that's what's dead, right? So in a lot of cases when we were talking to various customers as this blog post came out, most of our customers were like, yeah, issue tracking is dead. By the way, what are you guys? What am I buying?
turns.zh: 我们业务的好处在于，我们还没大到会杀死自己的程度，对吧？如果你是 Google，要杀死搜索业务可能真的很难，对吧？在每个搜索结果顶部放一个 AI 框，也许没人会看广告了，对吧？所以你的整个业务被颠覆了。是的，问题的单元仍然存在，但我们可能不应该有一个人们手动跟踪工作的世界。所以那才是已死的，对吧？所以很多情况下，当这篇博客文章发布时，我们与各种客户交谈，大多数客户都说，是的，问题跟踪已死。顺便问一下，你们是什么？我买的是什么？

turns.en: Christina Cordova, you're the COO of Linear. Could you introduce yourself?
turns.zh: Christina Cordova，你是 Linear 的 COO。能介绍一下你自己吗？

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. So I'm Christina. I've been at Linear for about three and a half years now. Joined as COO and I'm still COO today. Prior to Linear, I spent time at Notion leading our platform to build out our APIs and then our partnerships and self-serve growth initiatives as well. And then before that I was at Stripe for seven and a half years and there I led a lot of our early partnerships and go-to-market and then moved over to the product side and built out some new products for early stage companies. So I've been probably anywhere from the product side of a company and managing engineers all the way to managing the business side of a company as well, which has been really fun.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。我是 Christina。我在 Linear 大约三年半了。作为 COO 加入，现在仍然是 COO。在 Linear 之前，我在 Notion 负责平台，构建我们的 API，然后是合作伙伴关系和自助增长计划。再之前，我在 Stripe 工作了七年半，在那里我领导了许多早期的合作伙伴关系和市场推广，然后转到产品侧，为早期公司构建了一些新产品。所以我可能从公司的产品侧和管理工程师，一直到管理公司的业务侧，这真的很有趣。

turns.en: So why did Linear hire a COO at like 40 employees? Is that odd or is that pretty normal?
turns.zh: 那么为什么 Linear 在只有 40 名员工时就聘请了一位 COO？这奇怪吗，还是相当正常？

turns.en: I mean, I generally don't believe every company needs a COO, right? Like when I talk to founders and they're like, hey, I think I found product market fit. How do we start to scale the business side of the company? I am often, I feel like against maybe hiring someone like me. So I think for every company it's a little bit different. I think you have to really understand as a founder what are the things you need and what are the things you're looking for and the people that you bring onto the team. Often early on it's just like I need someone to sell something, right? We have expanded beyond the capability of the founder or CEO to sell every net new customer, right? So there I generally talk about well you should hire folks in sales, maybe hire a sales leader to build out a team, right? But if you're not exactly sure what you're looking for in marketing or operations or other parts of the company, then it may very well not make sense to hire someone like me. You know I think with the Linear founders, they were incredibly focused on design and engineering and product and I think they had a really great combination of skills between the three of them. But as we were starting to scale the business side of the company, they didn't necessarily look at the next salesperson that we hired and said hmm I know exactly what we're looking for here and I know whether or not sales is performing really well, right? So if you don't look at different parts of your company and say like okay I know what great is and I feel like I have a good sense of how to get to great, it can sometimes be helpful to hire someone like me or like a functional leader when it comes time to do that.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我通常不认为每家公司都需要 COO，对吧？比如当我与创始人交谈时，他们说，嘿，我想我找到了产品市场契合点。我们如何开始扩展公司的业务侧？我经常觉得可能不应该聘请像我这样的人。所以我认为每家公司都有一点不同。我认为作为创始人，你必须真正了解你需要什么，你在寻找什么，以及你带入团队的人。通常早期只是像我需要有人来卖东西，对吧？我们已经超出了创始人或 CEO 销售每个净新客户的能力，对吧？所以在那里我通常会说，你应该雇佣销售人员，也许雇佣一个销售负责人来组建团队，对吧？但如果你不确定你在市场营销或运营或公司其他部门寻找什么，那么聘请像我这样的人可能根本没有意义。你知道，我认为对于 Linear 的创始人来说，他们非常专注于设计、工程和产品，我认为他们三个人之间有非常好的技能组合。但当我们开始扩展公司的业务侧时，他们不一定看着我们雇佣的下一个销售人员说，嗯，我确切地知道我们在这里寻找什么，我知道销售是否表现良好，对吧？所以如果你不看公司的不同部门并说，好的，我知道什么是伟大的，我觉得我有很好的感觉如何达到伟大，那么有时聘请像我这样的人或职能领导者可能会有所帮助。

turns.en: Yeah, so like what did the business look like at that point? Like can you talk about like what revenue they were at or
turns.zh: 是的，那么当时业务是什么样子的？你能谈谈他们的收入是多少，或者

turns.en: Yeah, we were probably, I want to say, we had some large customers but no public company customers. Probably no customer above, I want to say, maybe 500 seats or something like that. So I would say we mostly tapped out at mid-market and we were probably best known for being a great product for startups, but not necessarily a great product for other companies at that time. You know and I think at that point in time we were doing well with a product-led growth model where most people were using our product because they signed up self-serve.
turns.zh: 是的，我们可能，我想说，我们有一些大客户，但没有上市公司客户。可能没有客户超过，我想说，也许 500 个席位左右。所以我会说我们主要在中端市场达到上限，我们可能最出名的是作为初创公司的好产品，但不一定是当时其他公司的好产品。你知道，我认为当时我们在产品主导的增长模式下做得很好，大多数人使用我们的产品是因为他们自助注册。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And then grew with us over time. So companies like Vercel and Ramp and many other customers like that really never talked to a human being at Linear, signed up for the product, started using it, and then started scaling, which was great. Like you know, the product can do a lot of work on its own, but it was also start like time to start selling to the company that is not even going to put a lick of data into your service without signing a contract and doing a pilot and surveying their team on what tool they're using before and what tool is this and what's better, right? So that was a very different kind of motion for the company to start scaling to larger companies and that was pretty much my objective. And we've at least 10 X I think since I joined. So.
turns.zh: 然后随着时间的推移与我们共同成长。所以像 Vercel 和 Ramp 以及许多其他类似的客户，真的从未与 Linear 的人交谈过，注册了产品，开始使用，然后开始扩展，这很棒。就像你知道的，产品可以自己完成很多工作，但也到了开始向那些如果不签合同、不做试点、不调查团队之前使用什么工具、这是什么工具、什么更好，就不会在你的服务中放入一点数据的公司销售的时候了，对吧？所以这对公司开始扩展到更大的公司来说是一种非常不同的方式，这几乎是我的目标。自从我加入以来，我们至少增长了 10 倍。所以。

turns.en: And you joined like four years ago?
turns.zh: 你大约四年前加入的？

turns.en: Uh three almost three and a half years ago.
turns.zh: 呃，三年，差不多三年半前。

turns.en: Oh okay. So I think the Linear founders have talked about this. I think you have as well that like before you join Linear, you always do a like a trial period.
turns.zh: 哦好的。所以我认为 Linear 的创始人谈过这个。我想你也谈过，就像在你加入 Linear 之前，你总是有一个试用期。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So did you also have to do a trial period?
turns.zh: 那么你也必须经历试用期吗？

turns.en: I did. Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。是的。

turns.en: Yeah like what was that like?
turns.zh: 是的，那是什么样的？

turns.en: Yeah. I mean I think my project was quite simple. It was something like come up with the go-to-market plan for Linear with a bounded time period like for the next six to 12 months or something like that, right? And I think the good thing about that is that, you know, that is the job. Like right? So you're not giving someone some fictional project that's not really representative of what they would do when they join the company. It's like a real project and that would effectively be my job in joining the company. So, you know, if they didn't like the outcomes that I produced as part of that project, they probably shouldn't hire me.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，我认为我的项目很简单。大概是制定 Linear 的市场推广计划，有明确的时间范围，比如未来 6 到 12 个月左右，对吧？我认为这样做的好处是，你知道，那就是工作。对吧？所以你不是给某人一个虚构的项目，不能真正代表他们加入公司后会做什么。这是一个真实项目，那实际上就是我加入公司后的工作。所以，你知道，如果他们不喜欢我在那个项目中产生的结果，他们可能不应该雇用我。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So I think it was a really good way of saying like I have some ideas of what the company can do better, but also I want to get feedback from the people who are on the ground. Like, you know, we had a salesperson on our team. We had someone doing customer success.
turns.zh: 所以我认为这是一个非常好的方式，可以说我有一些关于公司可以做得更好的想法，但我也想从一线人员那里获得反馈。就像，你知道，我们团队有一个销售人员。我们有做客户成功的人。

turns.en: We had some people doing support and one or two folks doing marketing, right? So getting their perspectives on different parts of the business and where I should focus and prioritize, and then making sure that the company was also bought in on that vision for the world, I think was really helpful for me. And then when I actually started at the company, it was almost like I had this little blueprint for what my job should be and what I should accomplish.
turns.zh: 我们有一些人做支持，一两个人做市场，对吧？所以从他们那里了解业务的不同部分、我应该关注和优先考虑的地方，然后确保公司也认同那个愿景，我觉得对我很有帮助。然后当我真正开始在公司工作时，几乎就像我有了这个小蓝图，知道我的工作应该是什么，我应该完成什么。

turns.en: Can you talk about what was in that plan?
turns.zh: 你能谈谈那个计划里有什么吗？

turns.en: I think a lot of it was brand and marketing oriented. So things around making Linear inevitable in a lot of ways. So either you're already on Linear or you should be planning your move to Linear effectively. And most companies that we want to acquire should be in one world or the other. So a lot of that was around driving the brand, building storytelling, increasing awareness for the company because I think we were well known, but I would say in particular niches, not really outside of that.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多都是品牌和市场导向的。所以很多事情是围绕让 Linear 不可避免。所以要么你已经在用 Linear，要么你应该有效地计划转向 Linear。而我们想要获取的大多数公司都应该在其中一个世界里。所以很多都是围绕推动品牌、构建故事、提高公司知名度，因为我觉得我们很有名，但我想说是在特定细分领域，而不是真正在那之外。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: So we were doing marketing, but the only marketing we were doing was sending out emails if we had a change log of something new that we released. And it turns out that less than 10% of users subscribed to emails. So most people didn't necessarily know even just the new features we were shipping, which was interesting. And then we would send a tweet.
turns.zh: 所以我们在做市场，但我们唯一做的市场就是如果有新发布的变更日志就发邮件。结果发现不到 10% 的用户订阅了邮件。所以大多数人甚至不知道我们正在发布的新功能，这很有趣。然后我们会发一条推文。

turns.en: Okay. Like from the founders' accounts or from the company account?
turns.zh: 好的。是从创始人的账户还是公司账户？

turns.en: Then the founders would reshare and they have their own pretty strong social presence as well. But that was the extent of it really. So a lot of it was just thinking about, okay, how are we telling a more holistic story in a better way? And then how are we actually reaching the people that we want to be reaching? It turns out that a lot of our users are in the app day to day. And so why are we not just giving them notifications about what's changing within the product, within the place they're already at every day, right? So just thinking about things that could be great ways to market to existing users or market to net new customers that also didn't feel off with the brand, right? So I spent a lot of time on that. A lot of it was also just growing the sales team. I think a lot of early stage companies especially that are engineering driven, product led growth oriented are like the product should sell itself and then everyone realizes that gets you to a certain point.
turns.zh: 然后创始人们会转发，他们自己也有很强的社交影响力。但真的就仅此而已。所以很多只是思考，好吧，我们如何以更好的方式讲述一个更全面的故事？然后我们如何真正触达我们想要触达的人？结果发现我们的很多用户每天都在应用里。那么为什么我们不直接给他们发通知，告诉他们产品内正在发生的变化，在他们每天已经在的地方，对吧？所以只是思考一些可以成为向现有用户营销或向净新客户营销的好方法，同时也不让人觉得与品牌不符，对吧？所以我花了很多时间在那上面。很多也是关于发展销售团队。我觉得很多早期公司，尤其是工程驱动、产品主导增长导向的，会觉得产品应该自我销售，然后每个人都意识到那只能让你达到某个点。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And then when you want to grow faster, you also need to start thinking about reaching people in different ways and not everyone buys products self-serve. And especially when you're choosing a system that's so core to your product development process, which we are. A lot of companies are not going to make that decision without building trust with human beings. And when I was doing my work trial, we had one person on sales, right?
turns.zh: 然后当你想更快增长时，你也需要开始思考以不同方式触达人们，不是每个人都自助购买产品。尤其是当你选择一个对产品开发流程如此核心的系统时，而我们就是。很多公司不会在没有与真人建立信任的情况下做出那个决定。当我做工作试用时，我们只有一个人做销售，对吧？

turns.en: So it was not you.
turns.zh: 所以不是你。

turns.en: So it was just like there's only so much you could do with one person, right?
turns.zh: 所以就像一个人能做的有限，对吧？

turns.en: Were they like an experienced salesperson?
turns.zh: 他们是有经验的销售人员吗？

turns.en: Yeah, yeah yeah yeah yeah. He's actually our sales leader today. So he leads our entire sales team. So he's great. But at the time I would say this wasn't really on him. It was more on the company. It's just like how do we actually think we want to grow this team, right? You can grow a sales team in lots of ways. You can have lots of SDRs. We don't have any SDRs. You can have forward deployed engineers now. That's very popular, right? We actually don't do forward deployed engineering. We have solutions engineers, which I think is distinct and somewhat different. But we added those later.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。他实际上是我们今天的销售负责人。所以他领导我们整个销售团队。所以他很棒。但当时我会说这并不真的怪他。这更多是公司的问题。就像我们到底认为我们想如何发展这个团队，对吧？你可以用很多方式发展销售团队。你可以有很多 SDR。我们没有任何 SDR。你现在可以有前置部署工程师。那很流行，对吧？我们实际上不做前置部署工程。我们有解决方案工程师，我认为那是不同的，有些不一样。但我们后来才加入那些。

turns.en: Part of the sales org?
turns.zh: 是销售组织的一部分吗？

turns.en: Yeah. We really optimized our team at the beginning for hiring AEs who had experience selling technical products. Because we knew if you had sold to a designer, if you had sold to an engineer before, we wouldn't necessarily have to teach you how to do that. And I think selling to someone who's very discerning, doesn't want to see your fancy slides, just wants to get into a demo, is very different from selling to a person in, I don't know, people ops or something else. So looking for people with that very explicit experience and then making sure that we could onboard them and train them and get them really competent in the product itself.
turns.zh: 是的。我们一开始真的优化了团队，招聘有销售技术产品经验的 AE。因为我们知道如果你曾经向设计师销售过，如果你曾经向工程师销售过，我们就不一定需要教你如何做。而且我觉得向一个非常挑剔、不想看你的花哨幻灯片、只想进入演示的人销售，与向一个人力运营或其他什么的人销售非常不同。所以寻找有那种非常明确经验的人，然后确保我们能够入职培训他们，让他们真正精通产品本身。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Because that's required to build trust with our customer, right? So just figuring out what's different about this company and what's going to be different about hiring or scaling, and also what's the way that the founders want to do it and can we do that? So support is an interesting example. When I was interviewing, the founders were very clear that they did not want to outsource support. And I've never worked at a company that didn't outsource support. So that was like okay.
turns.zh: 因为那是与客户建立信任所必需的，对吧？所以只是弄清楚这家公司有什么不同，招聘或扩展会有什么不同，还有创始人想要的方式是什么，我们能这样做吗？所以支持是一个有趣的例子。当我面试时，创始人非常清楚他们不想外包支持。而我从未在一家不外包支持的公司工作过。所以那就像好吧。

turns.en: Does it internally, right?
turns.zh: 内部做，对吧？

turns.en: No, they outsource. Yeah. Unless something's changed since I was there, but they have internal folks who work on support too. But they do outsource. So I think for us, that was something that we really wanted to maintain because we really cared about delivering a high quality experience, delivering a fast experience, and knowing that for a long time we didn't have a sales team, right? So because we didn't have that, we knew that your first touch point often if you want to talk to a human being was going to be support. So the support better be good, right? And so we've still been able to figure out how to scale the team today into a global team that does not outsource at all. So we'll see what the future brings. Never say never on any of these things. But there are certain ways that we want to do things and we probably want to do them for as long as possible as long as it's feasible for the business and makes sense.
turns.zh: 不，他们外包。是的。除非我离开后有什么变化，但他们也有内部人员做支持。但他们确实外包。所以我觉得对我们来说，那是我们真正想要保持的，因为我们真的关心提供高质量体验、快速体验，并且知道很长一段时间我们没有销售团队，对吧？所以因为我们没有那个，我们知道如果你想和真人交谈，你的第一个接触点通常是支持。所以支持最好要好，对吧？所以我们仍然能够弄清楚如何将团队扩展成今天一个完全不外包的全球团队。所以我们看看未来会怎样。永远别说永不。但我们有某些做事方式，我们可能想尽可能长时间地这样做，只要对业务可行且合理。

turns.en: Yeah. So when you first joined, I guess I've never been in a sales role, but do you have to say, okay, we're starting with startups and we can't just immediately go to big enterprises and start selling them. We have to go step by step.
turns.zh: 是的。那么当你刚加入时，我想我从未担任过销售角色，但你是否必须说，好吧，我们从初创公司开始，我们不能立即去找大企业并向他们销售。我们必须一步一步来。

turns.en: So did you have to go, oh, we have to first get medium-sized businesses and then at some point we'll go enterprise? Like how does that work?
turns.zh: 所以你们是不是必须得先搞定中型企业，然后某个时候再进军大企业？这到底是怎么运作的？

turns.en: Yeah. So when I joined Linear, I think we had like three goals, like three company-level goals. And I think one of them was like move up market to enterprise. And then we had like a company offsite three weeks after I joined. And I like got up in front of the whole company, which was like I don't know, 35, 40 people at the time. And like I showed the slide of the three goals and I like crossed the one that says we're going to go after enterprises out.
turns.zh: 是的。当我加入 Linear 时，我们大概有三个目标，三个公司级的目标。其中一个就是向上市场进军，做企业级。然后在我加入三周后，我们有一个公司团建。我站在全公司面前，当时大概有 35、40 人吧。我展示了那三个目标的幻灯片，然后把那个说我们要进军企业级的目标划掉了。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: Because I was like, we have one person. We have literally one person on sales. You know, you're not going up market to enterprise with one person.
turns.zh: 因为我说，我们只有一个人。我们销售团队真的只有一个人。你知道，靠一个人是不可能向上市场进军企业级的。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So you have to think about what are you capable of doing? What do you need to learn in order to get there? And then do you actually have the resources to accomplish that goal, right? And I don't think we had any of those things at that period of time. We had companies that we had primarily won because they had scaled into being a growth-stage business or a mid-market business effectively, but we hadn't done a lot of acquiring net new mid-market companies at that point. So I changed that goal to say, no, we're going to go after companies in the growth segment. And that's going to be our goal. And if we can win a lot of companies who are in the growth segment, who already have a tool that does in some ways what we do, and we have to go in and convince them to rip that out and replace it with Linear, then if we're able to do that, that gives me the confidence to say that in a year or in two years we're going to be able to go after enterprises. But I don't have confidence in that now, so why would I set that as a goal for the team?
turns.zh: 所以你必须思考：你现在能做什么？你需要学习什么才能达到目标？然后你是否有足够的资源来实现那个目标？我认为当时我们这些条件都不具备。我们赢得的公司主要是那些已经成长为增长阶段或中型市场的公司，但那时我们并没有大量获取新的中型市场客户。所以我把目标改为：不，我们要瞄准增长阶段的公司。这就是我们的目标。如果我们能赢得许多增长阶段的公司，这些公司已经有某种工具在某种程度上做着我们做的事情，我们必须进去说服他们放弃那个工具，换成 Linear，如果我们能做到这一点，这让我有信心说，一年或两年后我们能够进军企业级。但现在我没有信心，那为什么要把这个设成团队的目标呢？

turns.en: Completely agree. It's really about setting those baby steps and making sure that you're doing well with companies that you can serve today incredibly well, so that those companies when they're getting the reference calls from the larger companies being like, "Hey, do you like Linear and has your experience been good?" They're saying really positive things. And that helps us land the net new customer. And it worked very similarly when I was at Stripe. We did not win a lot of net new companies that were switching over from a competitor for a long time. We did a great job winning every net new business that was created. So like a startup that's implementing payments for the first time. And then we kind of started to win companies who were switching over. And some of that stuff just takes time. It's very different to sell a product where you have to rip technology out that already exists and replace it than just to sell something that's nice and shiny and new on top of an existing set of systems. So knowing that I was in a very similar position in this role, it was important that I just oriented the team around what I felt was a solvable problem. And then only in 2025, so that was 2023, only in 2025 did I go up in front of the company and say we're going after enterprise this year. And that was when we started our enterprise sales segment and built out that team.
turns.zh: 完全同意。这真的就是设定那些小步骤，确保你能服务好今天能服务好的公司，这样当那些公司接到大公司的推荐电话，问“嘿，你喜欢 Linear 吗？体验好吗？”时，他们会说非常正面的话。这帮助我们赢得新客户。我在 Stripe 时也是类似的情况。很长一段时间，我们并没有赢得很多从竞争对手转换过来的新公司。我们在赢得每一个新创企业方面做得很好，比如第一次实施支付的初创公司。然后我们开始赢得一些转换过来的公司。有些事就是需要时间。销售一个需要替换现有技术的产品，和销售一个在现有系统之上锦上添花的新产品，是非常不同的。所以知道我在这个职位上处于非常相似的位置，重要的是我把团队引导到我认为可解决的问题上。然后直到 2025 年——那是 2023 年——直到 2025 年，我才站在公司面前说我们今年要进军企业级。那时我们开始了企业销售部门并组建了那个团队。

turns.en: So okay, you guys are going after medium-sized businesses. And so you are getting everyone to basically, because most companies have an issue tracker, right?
turns.zh: 所以好吧，你们在瞄准中型企业。所以你们基本上要让每个人——因为大多数公司都有问题追踪工具，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah. Or some kind of tool to track it.
turns.zh: 是的。或者某种追踪工具。

turns.en: Like rip them away from them. So yeah, like how do you convince them to say, oh yeah, we're using XYZ product. It works for us, but uh yeah, like you know, pitch me basically.
turns.zh: 就像把他们从那些工具上剥离。所以是啊，你怎么说服他们说，哦对，我们在用 XYZ 产品，它对我们有效，但是呃，是啊，你知道，基本上就是向我推销吧。

turns.en: Yeah. And in the early days, it was about being significantly better than what the alternative solutions were. I don't think you can be 20% better, 30% better and get people to switch because there's a switching cost involved. So I think you have to figure out how you articulate how your product is better than what is already serving the market reasonably well, reasonably well enough that they have a lot of companies using their product. But the good thing about the space that we were entering, and I think one of the reasons why the Linear founders chose this space, were because they were all users of those legacy tools. When they were working at Coinbase and Airbnb and Uber. And so they knew no one liked these tools. And when they were getting rolled out at their companies, they were like, no, the fun time is going away. We have to start using these tools. So in a lot of ways it really helped that they had this knowledge and existing awareness of the feeling that came with the competitors in our space and could figure out how to build a product that got people really excited to manage their work, which is presumably not something that you would expect. So a lot of the emphasis in what we built early on was in design and UX. Make it a product that people want to be in every day and have to use. The hard part about that is that people have to try it before they get it, versus seeing a couple slides in a sales deck and being like, okay, I get it. So one of the things that we did, I think very well strategically, was just having a product that anyone could start using. So a free product initially that once you hit certain limits in terms of usage, you would have to start paying for. So a lot of people who started to use Linear for their company actually were just playing around with it for their own purposes for free and got a sense of how usable it was and how much easier it would be to utilize the product compared to competitors. So we started very much there and I think that worked well for a period of time. Now our approach in terms of how we sell Linear is very different. We're typically talking to companies about the sea change in the space that has happened over the last year and a half, two years in terms of your entire product development process has been upended. The way that you build products has completely changed. And it doesn't make sense anymore to live in a world where you have a manual way of saying, oh, I found a bug. Oh, I'm going to report that bug into my issue tracker. Oh, I'm going to label it and assign it to this other person.
turns.zh: 是的。在早期，关键是要比替代方案好得多。我不认为你能只好 20%、30% 就让人们转换，因为存在转换成本。所以我认为你必须弄清楚如何阐述你的产品比那些已经相当好地服务市场的产品更好——好到有很多公司在用他们的产品。但我们进入的这个领域的好处在于，我认为 Linear 创始人选择这个领域的原因之一，是因为他们都是那些传统工具的用户。当他们在 Coinbase、Airbnb 和 Uber 工作时，他们知道没人喜欢这些工具。当这些工具在他们公司推广时，他们就想，不，快乐时光结束了，我们得开始用这些工具了。所以从很多方面来说，他们拥有这种认知和对竞争对手带来的感受的现有意识，真的很有帮助，并且能够弄清楚如何构建一个让人们真正兴奋地管理工作的产品，这大概不是你预期的事情。所以我们早期构建的产品非常强调设计和用户体验。让它成为一个人们每天都想用、不得不用产品。难处在于人们必须试用才能理解，而不是看销售演示文稿里的几页幻灯片就说，好的，我懂了。所以我们做得很好的一件事，我认为在战略上，就是有一个任何人都可以开始使用的产品。所以最初是免费产品，一旦达到一定的使用限制，你就需要开始付费。所以很多开始为公司使用 Linear 的人，实际上只是免费为自己玩玩，并感受到了它的可用性，以及相比竞争对手使用起来容易多少。所以我们从那里开始，我认为在一段时间内效果很好。现在我们销售 Linear 的方式非常不同。我们通常和公司谈论过去一年半到两年这个领域发生的巨变，即你的整个产品开发流程已经被颠覆。你构建产品的方式已经完全改变了。现在再生活在一个你手动地说“哦，我发现了一个 bug。哦，我要把那个 bug 报告到我的问题追踪器里。哦，我要给它打标签并分配给另一个人”的世界里，已经不合理了。

turns.en: And then that person is going to fix it and add a status update and then close it and then notify the customer. And every step in that path is completely manual. It just doesn't make any sense for the world that we live in now. And you talk to most companies and they're like, yes, I completely agree. And so we really oriented the company in the last year and a half around agents and agents performing a lot of the parts of the workflow that are effectively not product development. Like everything I described in that whole chain is not you building products. And so if you can make Linear a really great tool for agentic workflows, then the individual engineer, the individual PM, or designer who's using Linear can ultimately be spending more of their time building products and less time manually moving around work in a system to prove that they are adding value to a company.
turns.zh: 然后那个人会去修复它，添加状态更新，然后关闭它，再通知客户。这条路径上的每一步都是完全手动的。这在我们如今生活的世界里根本说不通。你和大多数公司聊，他们都会说，是的，我完全同意。所以过去一年半，我们真的把公司围绕智能体来定位，让智能体执行工作流中大量实际上不属于产品开发的部分。就像我描述的那整个链条，都不是你在构建产品。所以如果你能让 Linear 成为智能体式工作流的绝佳工具，那么使用 Linear 的个体工程师、个体产品经理或设计师，最终就能把更多时间花在构建产品上，更少时间花在手动在系统里搬动工作以证明自己对公司有价值上。

turns.en: Yeah, that's really interesting because it seems like the pitch early on was the user experience, right? And now it seems like the humans are not going to be interacting with the UI.
turns.zh: 是的，这真的很有趣，因为早期的卖点似乎是用户体验，对吧？而现在看起来人类将不再与 UI 交互了。

turns.en: I actually think that a lot of companies right now are feeling like it's going to be okay to just be like a database and have an MCP server and give all of their data away to agents and have the agents interoperate with them and think that that's going to be a great business model. And I don't think that's going to be a great business model ultimately.
turns.zh: 我实际上认为，现在很多公司觉得，仅仅做一个数据库、有一个 MCP 服务器、把所有数据都交给智能体、让智能体与它们互操作，这样就可以了，并认为这会是一个伟大的商业模式。但我不认为这最终会是一个伟大的商业模式。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: I think you have to bring the agentic workflows into your tools and you have to make them better than the tools that people would be using externally to interoperate with your system. Otherwise, there's no reason for people to go into your tool, right? And so for us, the metric that we're typically looking at—and we've seen a lot of change here—we launched our MCP server in 2025. I think we were basically the first company in our space to do it. And now over 50% of issues created on Linear are created by agents in just like a year and a half. Half the work is created in an entirely different way than it was before. So that kind of illustrates how much has changed in a pretty short period of time. And then when we look at how many users are coming to the app and integrating or creating issues within the app itself, that's also going up significantly.
turns.zh: 我认为你必须把智能体式工作流引入你的工具，并且让它们比人们外部使用的、用来与你的系统互操作的工具更好。否则，人们就没有理由进入你的工具，对吧？所以对我们来说，我们通常关注的指标——我们在这里看到了很多变化——我们在 2025 年推出了 MCP 服务器。我想我们基本上是业内第一家这么做的公司。而现在，Linear 上创建的问题中超过 50% 是由智能体创建的，仅仅一年半时间。一半的工作是以与以前完全不同的方式创建的。所以这在一定程度上说明了在相当短的时间内发生了多大的变化。然后当我们看有多少用户来到应用并在应用内集成或创建问题时，这个数字也在显著上升。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: Right? So sometimes people believe that, oh, I'm just using MCP server for everything now. But you are also going back to the app and you're interacting with it because you need to visualize things, and often a chat interface isn't the best way to visualize all the work that a team is doing. It's not great for collaboration because it's typically single-player only. And so I think for us, as long as the MCP usage line and the app usage line are kind of going up into the right together, it proves that we have both a great UX that's great for humans and also great for agents. And that's our goal, I think, as a product: that you can be great at both of those things. And it doesn't mean that now that agents exist, you don't have to care about the interface.
turns.zh: 对吧？所以有时候人们认为，哦，我现在所有事情都只用 MCP 服务器。但你也会回到应用里与它交互，因为你需要可视化东西，而聊天界面往往不是可视化团队所有工作的最佳方式。它也不利于协作，因为它通常只支持单人使用。所以我认为对我们来说，只要 MCP 使用曲线和应用使用曲线一起向右上方走，就证明我们既有对人类很棒的 UX，也有对智能体很棒的 UX。我认为这就是我们作为产品的目标：你可以在两方面都做得很好。这并不意味着有了智能体，你就不必关心界面了。

turns.en: Mhm. And app usage is measured by just number of people using it? Because I'm assuming also your customer base is just growing, right? So how do you—
turns.zh: 嗯。应用使用量只是用使用人数来衡量吗？因为我猜你的客户群也在增长，对吧？所以你怎么——

turns.en: Work created in the application. So our unit of work, the smallest unit of work is the issue, right? So if you just look at work created, that's a human going into the app—our mobile app, our desktop app, our web app, all of those places—and creating work. If you look at how the work is moving through the pipeline, like getting assigned to an agent, sometimes that's done manually by a human, sometimes an agent does it when it assigns or delegates to another agent.
turns.zh: 是在应用中创建的工作。我们的工作单元，最小的工作单元是问题，对吧？所以如果你只看创建的工作，那是人类进入应用——我们的移动应用、桌面应用、网页应用，所有这些地方——并创建工作。如果你看工作如何在流程中移动，比如分配给智能体，有时是由人类手动完成的，有时是智能体在分配或委托给另一个智能体时完成的。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Often we're now part of the workflow. You can use a feature we have called Loops that will automatically assign an agent to a given issue and have the agent start coding against it, for example. So in a lot of cases it's an agent doing the work, but it's a Linear agent,
turns.zh: 现在我们常常是工作流的一部分。你可以使用我们称为 Loops 的功能，它会自动将智能体分配给某个问题，并让智能体开始针对它编码，例如。所以在很多情况下，是智能体在做工作，但它是 Linear 智能体，

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: right? Which we also want to see. So we have to look at multiple different factors. But it's generally app sessions that we're looking at in terms of trying to understand activity.
turns.zh: 对吧？这也是我们希望看到的。所以我们必须看多个不同的因素。但一般来说，我们看的是应用会话，以了解活动情况。

turns.en: Yeah. So I guess that leads me to Kari writing this blog post like issue tracking is dead. So I'm assuming you were in the middle of selling some contracts when he wrote that. So how do you explain to your customers that, hey, our entire business was issue tracking before and now our CEO just wrote this blog post? Yeah, like how do you explain that to them and how did that transition happen?
turns.zh: 是的。所以我想这就引出了 Kari 写的那篇博文，说问题跟踪已死。所以我猜他写那篇博文时，你正在谈一些合同。那么你怎么向客户解释，嘿，我们整个业务以前就是问题跟踪，现在我们 CEO 刚写了这篇博文？是的，你怎么向他们解释，这个转变是怎么发生的？

turns.en: Yeah. Well, I think the great thing about our business is that we're not so big to kill ourselves, right? It's probably really hard if you're Google to kill the search business and put an AI box at the top of every search result and maybe no one's going to look at the ads, right? So your entire business is upended. And so I think that's a little bit of the innovator's dilemma challenge that a lot of tools that were pre-AI have, and we were certainly one of those companies that was pre-AI. And so for us the great thing is that it's like, okay, we see that the world is going in this direction and you can either lean into it with the plan that you build the best product for the new era
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，我认为我们业务的好处在于，我们还没大到会杀死自己，对吧？如果你是 Google，要杀死搜索业务可能真的很难，在每个搜索结果顶部放一个 AI 框，也许就没人看广告了，对吧？所以你的整个业务就被颠覆了。所以我认为这有点像是许多前 AI 时代的工具所面临的创新者窘境挑战，而我们当然是那些前 AI 时代的公司之一。所以对我们来说，好处在于，好吧，我们看到世界正朝这个方向走，你要么全力投入，制定计划为新时代打造最好的产品，

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: rather than trying to hold on to an era that is probably not going to exist in a few years, right? So if the workflow that I talked about with this manual intervention by humans at every step of the process is not going to be the work that we live in. You look at Linear now and yes, the unit of the issue still exists, but we probably shouldn't have a world where people are manually tracking work.
turns.zh: 而不是试图抓住一个可能几年后就不存在的时代，对吧？所以如果我谈到的那个在每个步骤都需要人类手动干预的工作流，不会成为我们未来所处的工作方式。你现在看 Linear，是的，问题的单元仍然存在，但我们可能不应该有一个人们手动跟踪工作的世界。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So that's what's dead, right? So in a lot of cases when we were talking to various customers as this blog post came out, most of our customers were like, yeah, issue tracking is dead. And by the way, what are you guys? What am I buying? And so it's much more oriented around now being a product development system. We want you to focus on building better products and we are going to build a system that enables you to do so with very little manual work.
turns.zh: 所以这就是已死的东西，对吧？所以在很多情况下，当这篇博文发布时，我们与各种客户交谈，大多数客户都说，是的，问题跟踪已死。顺便问一下，你们是什么？我买的是什么？所以现在它更多是围绕成为一个产品开发系统。我们希望你们专注于构建更好的产品，而我们将构建一个系统，让你们能够以极少的手动工作做到这一点。

turns.en: So, it's also about saying, 'We're going to create a new category,' and yes, we will in a lot of ways still play in the old category, but we are also driving the vast majority of our resources as a team into this new category of things like agent orchestration, managing work in a way where you don't necessarily have to be doing a lot of manual work, taking tasks through a system, and then you're operating far more agentically, both within Linear and also outside of Linear.
turns.zh: 所以，这也是在说：“我们要创建一个新品类。”是的，在很多方面我们仍会在旧品类中竞争，但作为团队，我们也将绝大部分资源投入到这个新品类中，比如智能体编排、以你不必做大量手动工作的方式管理工作——把任务通过系统流转——然后你就能在 Linear 内外都以更加智能体式的方式运作。

turns.en: So I guess that transition or that blog post—were you blindsided by Karri writing that, or was everyone on the same page?
turns.zh: 那么我猜那个转变或者那篇博客文章——Karri 写那个的时候你感到意外吗，还是大家意见一致？

turns.en: We were on the same page.
turns.zh: 我们意见一致。

turns.en: So were you seeing your customers asking for that, or was it that you wanted to push your customers that way?
turns.zh: 所以你是看到客户在要求这个，还是你想推动客户往那个方向走？

turns.en: I think some of our customers were asking for this. Linear is used by the vast majority of all the frontier AI labs as an example. The vast majority of top AI companies already use Linear. So if you look at that customer set, this kind of net new generation of companies that started after Linear, many of those companies were saying, 'This is the way that we're going, and we want Linear to move in that direction. Otherwise, it's not going to be the right product for us.' And then at the same time, we also saw with companies that were pre-AI—examples might be companies like Ramp or Coinbase—where they existed before all of this and decided that they were going to invest their own internal teams to build internal agents to do work with them. And so we were like, 'Hey, we actually need an API that enables you to create agents within Linear.' So if you're one of these companies that is almost pre-AI but on the bleeding edge of AI still, and you're creating your own bespoke agent to help manage various different types of work or code internally, and you want to own the proprietary data that's associated with that, we want to build the API so that you can deeply integrate Linear with those tools. And there wasn't a system or a set of APIs that any of our competitors had at the time for that. So again, just being first to build a lot of these new ways of interacting with Linear, formats of agent workflows, and then building agents directly into Linear as well—I think we're all very new for us, and some customers were asking us for them, and I would say a lot of customers weren't. But I can tell you that now a lot of them are very happy that we have a lot of these features, because not every company is on the bleeding edge of the way that product development is changing.
turns.zh: 我认为我们的一些客户在要求这个。举个例子，Linear 被绝大多数前沿 AI 实验室使用。绝大多数顶尖 AI 公司已经在用 Linear。所以如果你看那个客户群，也就是在 Linear 之后起步的新一代公司，很多公司都在说：“这就是我们前进的方向，我们希望 Linear 往那个方向走。否则，它就不是适合我们的产品。”同时，我们也看到一些前 AI 时代的公司——比如 Ramp 或 Coinbase——它们在这一切之前就存在，并决定投入自己的内部团队来构建内部智能体与它们协同工作。于是我们说：“嘿，我们其实需要一个 API，让你能在 Linear 内创建智能体。”所以，如果你是这类几乎属于前 AI 时代但仍处于 AI 前沿的公司，并且你正在创建自己的定制智能体来帮助管理内部各种不同类型的工作或代码，并且你想拥有与之相关的专有数据，我们就想构建这个 API，让你能将 Linear 与那些工具深度集成。当时我们的竞争对手都没有这样的系统或一套 API。所以，再次强调，率先构建许多与 Linear 交互的新方式、智能体工作流的格式，以及将智能体直接构建到 Linear 中——我认为这对我们来说都很新，有些客户在要求这些功能，我得说很多客户并没有。但我可以告诉你，现在很多客户非常高兴我们有了这些功能，因为并非每家公司都处于产品开发方式变革的前沿。

turns.en: I guess that's what I was trying to get at—I'm assuming because you were trying to go more enterprise, a lot of them were those legacy type companies, right?
turns.zh: 我猜这就是我想说的——我假设因为你们想更偏向企业级，很多客户是那种传统型公司，对吧？

turns.en: Yes, yes. And not the kinds of companies that are really pushing us in this direction. But now those are the companies that are reaching out to us and saying, 'Hey, a lot of the way that we're doing things has changed, and the systems that we use to build products should be changing just as rapidly as the landscape of coding agents, as an example. And if you feel like your underlying tool set hasn't really changed, hasn't really evolved in this new world, then you should probably think about changing your tool set, right?'
turns.zh: 是的，是的。而且不是那些真正推动我们朝这个方向走的公司。但现在正是那些公司在联系我们说：“嘿，我们做事的很多方式已经变了，我们用来构建产品的系统应该像编码智能体的格局一样快速变化。如果你觉得你的底层工具集在这个新世界里没有真正改变、没有真正进化，那么你大概应该考虑更换你的工具集了，对吧？”

turns.en: So when you start building these new features, how do you teach your customers how to use those features? I mean, how did you guys do that?
turns.zh: 那么当你们开始构建这些新功能时，你们如何教客户使用这些功能？我是说，你们是怎么做的？

turns.en: Yes, yes. So one, I would say, again, we really emphasize with functions like sales and customer success that they understand the product very deeply. And we really try to get our sales and success teams to share learnings with each other. So a lot of our calls are recorded with Gong as an example, and often our own customers will be screen sharing their workflows with us. And then we get to take that as a learning to say, 'Here's how this company is doing it. Really interesting. Maybe I can take that to another customer.' So there's both learning from your customers—which, when you have customers who are builders, you should always think about how you're going to learn from them versus purely just how you're going to teach them.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。所以第一，我得说，我们再次强调销售和客户成功等职能要非常深入地理解产品。我们真的努力让销售和成功团队相互分享经验。比如，我们的很多通话都用 Gong 录制，我们的客户经常通过屏幕共享向我们展示他们的工作流。然后我们把它作为学习材料说：“这家公司是这样做的，很有意思。也许我可以把这个带给另一个客户。”所以既有向客户学习——当你的客户是构建者时，你应该始终考虑如何向他们学习，而不仅仅是纯粹如何教他们。

turns.en: It's nice to have AI labs as customers.
turns.zh: 有 AI 实验室作为客户真好。

turns.en: Exactly, exactly. And then you're taking those learnings and you're saying, 'Hmm, how do I package this up for a user that is maybe not at that point yet?' And then, for example, we had customers who were like, 'Oh yeah, wouldn't it be great if there was an agent that existed that would triage everything for me?' Because nobody wants to groom their backlog, right? Like what a task that feels so outdated, right? And so we built a feature called Triage Intelligence, which effectively enables anything that comes into your triage workflow—bug reports, feature requests, etc.—to be automatically labeled, assigned, put on the right team's queue, and you as a human do not have to do anything for that to take place. So it's like you don't need to build an agent for this. We can just do it for you. So not everything necessarily needs to be an agent. It can just be part of the product. So it's both taught us how to teach the next customer how to do things better, but it's also helped us incorporate that into the product itself.
turns.zh: 正是，正是。然后你把这些经验拿来，说：“嗯，我如何为可能还没到那个阶段的用户打包这个？”然后，例如，我们有客户说：“哦对，如果有一个智能体能帮我分类所有事情，那该多好？”因为没人想整理他们的待办列表，对吧？这任务感觉太落伍了，对吧？所以我们构建了一个叫 Triage Intelligence 的功能，它有效地让进入你分类工作流的任何东西——错误报告、功能请求等——自动被标记、分配、放到正确团队的队列中，而你作为人类不需要做任何事情就能实现。所以就像你不需要为此构建一个智能体。我们可以直接为你做。所以并非所有东西都必须是智能体。它可以只是产品的一部分。所以这既教会了我们如何教下一个客户更好地做事，也帮助我们将这一点融入产品本身。

turns.en: And then it becomes far more easy for a person on our team to sell.
turns.zh: 然后我们团队的人销售起来就容易多了。

turns.en: So how does that work if, like, how do you teach sales people how to use engineering tools?
turns.zh: 那么这是怎么运作的，比如你如何教销售人员使用工程工具？

turns.en: Oh, well the great thing about Linear is that anyone can use it. Like, if I think about GitHub issues or something, when I go into GitHub, I'm like, 'Oh, as someone who's not an engineer, I'm going to mess something up. I don't belong here.' But I think the great thing about what we do is that that's not true. We try to create a product that's incredibly usable and well designed, not just for engineers, but really for anyone.
turns.zh: 哦，Linear 的伟大之处在于任何人都可以使用它。比如，如果我想到 GitHub issues 之类的，当我进入 GitHub 时，我会想：“哦，作为一个不是工程师的人，我会搞砸的。我不属于这里。”但我认为我们所做的事情的伟大之处在于，事实并非如此。我们试图创建一个极其易用且设计精良的产品，不仅为工程师，而是为任何人。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Right? And so now increasingly we're getting rolled out across wall-to-wall within organizations. So teams like sales and ops and anyone who wants to know what's on the product roadmap or be an input into what's on the product roadmap is using our product.
turns.zh: 对吧？所以现在越来越多地在组织内部全面推广。所以像销售和运营团队，以及任何想知道产品路线图内容或想为产品路线图提供输入的人，都在使用我们的产品。

turns.en: And it's very usable for them too, right? So I think that makes things far easier, just because it's not scary as a system or a tool. And our sales people have learned that just by being at the company we do a lot, as you can imagine, in Linear. So they need to know how to use it just to be at the company generally. And then again, a lot of it is in great training of your people. I think we've invested a lot in enablement. You effectively have to go through various coursework in order to be certified to even sell Linear and get on a call solo with the customer. So we really require that our sales reps understand a lot about the product. And maybe the most complex engineering workflow would probably be our code reviews product or our GitHub integration. Those can be somewhat complicated, often because you have to set up GitHub and have a demo GitHub workspace and a demo Linear workspace and make sure that they all work together. That can be a little bit more complex, but most of that is in relying on another tool and an integration workflow with it. But I think the great thing is now we have sales people on our team shipping copy edits to the website, and we have marketers on my team who are deciding, oh, we want to change how we store this data so that we have a better sense of what this revenue operations system does. And things like that are now accessible to everyone. And an engineer on our team just has to review that change and approve it. And I think it's also making Linear the product and what we do far more accessible to them too. But yeah, it takes time.
turns.zh: 而且这对他们来说也很好用，对吧？所以我觉得这让事情容易多了，因为它作为一个系统或工具并不吓人。我们的销售人员也学到了，只要待在公司里，我们在 Linear 里做的事情就很多，你可以想象。所以他们光是待在公司，就得知道怎么用它。然后，很大程度上还在于对员工进行良好的培训。我觉得我们在赋能上投入了很多。你实际上得完成各种课程，才能获得认证去卖 Linear，才能单独和客户通话。所以我们真的要求销售代表对产品有很深的了解。也许最复杂的工程工作流大概是我们的代码审查产品或者我们的 GitHub 集成。那些可能会有点复杂，通常是因为你得设置 GitHub，得有一个演示用的 GitHub 工作区和演示用的 Linear 工作区，还要确保它们能协同工作。那可能会稍微复杂一点，但大部分都依赖于另一个工具以及和它的集成工作流。不过我觉得很棒的一点是，现在我们团队里有销售人员在给网站提交文案修改，我团队里的市场人员也在决定，哦，我们想改变存储这些数据的方式，这样就能更好地理解这个营收运营系统在做什么。这类事情现在对所有人都触手可及。我们团队里的工程师只需要审查那个改动并批准它。我觉得这也让 Linear 这个产品和我们做的事情对他们来说更加触手可及。但没错，这需要时间。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.en: Like with anything.
turns.zh: 就像任何事情一样。

ts.sec: Team composition and the SDR question

turns.en: So is your team composition changing? Because now you're having different teams push copy updates to the website that maybe normally wouldn't have done that. And maybe are you seeing customer team compositions changing because of how they're using Linear, or just agentic development in general?
turns.zh: 那你们的团队构成在变化吗？因为现在你让不同的团队去给网站推送文案更新，而这些团队以前可能不会做这种事。也许你还看到客户的团队构成也在变化，因为他们使用 Linear 的方式，或者只是因为智能体式开发的大趋势？

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think one of the things that people are talking about a lot today is effectively how teams are changing in that they're remaining smaller, flatter, etc. I feel like there have been a lot of companies that aim to work that way for a period of time and then they just grow out of it and it changes. I think luckily, as a lot of these developments in our space were happening, Linear was already operating that way and has continued to operate that way, a lot of which can be due to AI. But I think as an example, other teams do this differently. We've never had SDRs, as an example, and I think that comes from a belief that a salesperson should be able to write an outbound email. Like I don't see why.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得现在大家谈论很多的一件事，就是团队实际上在如何变化——它们保持更小、更扁平等等。我感觉有很多公司有一段时间想那样运作，然后它们就发展得超出了那种模式，情况就变了。我觉得幸运的是，当这个领域的很多发展发生时，Linear 已经是那样运作的，并且一直那样运作，其中很多可能要归功于 AI。但举个例子，其他团队的做法不同。比如说，我们从来没有 SDR。我觉得这来自一个信念：销售人员应该能够自己写外联邮件。我不明白为什么不能。

turns.en: So what do SDRs normally do?
turns.zh: 那 SDR 通常做什么？

turns.en: Typically they're either doing outbound to new prospective customers and trying to get them in the pipeline, or they're qualifying those customers as they come in. So they'll do the first call. But unfortunately that first call is very not useful to the customer, because the rep is just being like, so how big are you? And how much money do you think you might be able to pay us, right? And again, our customer would hate to be on that call. They're like, why are you asking me questions? You are supposed to give me a demo, right? Why am I wasting 30 minutes of my time on this call just to get to a person who can give me a demo? So we don't have that function because I don't think it works well for our customers. But also because you can create systems and tooling and automatons that make it easier for an AE to do outbound to a customer. That feels like custom and useful, and is able to ultimately get some point of engagement. So that's one maybe difference between us and other companies. I think we've also opted to think about areas of the business where we can have fewer employees and what can you optimize with tooling. So our customer experience team is a great example. What are the tools that we can use to automatically draft replies to customers that write into us?
turns.zh: 通常他们要么是对新的潜在客户做外联，试图把他们引入销售管道，要么是在客户进来时对他们进行资格筛选。所以他们会打第一通电话。但不幸的是，那第一通电话对客户来说非常没用，因为销售代表只是在问，你们公司多大？你觉得你们能付我们多少钱，对吧？而且，我们的客户会讨厌打那通电话。他们会想，你为什么要问我问题？你应该给我做演示，对吧？我为什么要浪费 30 分钟在这通电话上，只为了能接触到那个能给我做演示的人？所以我们没有这个职能，因为我觉得它对我们的客户效果不好。但也因为你可以创建系统和工具以及自动化，让 AE 更容易对客户做外联。那感觉是定制化的、有用的，并且最终能够达成某种接触点。所以这可能是我们和其他公司的一个不同之处。我觉得我们还选择去思考业务中哪些领域可以用更少的员工，以及可以用工具优化什么。我们的客户体验团队就是一个很好的例子。我们可以用什么工具来自动起草回复给写信给我们的客户？

ts.sec: AI in support and avoiding slop

turns.en: Do you not see that having LLMs write stuff to customers produce slop? Like AI slop? Like how do you fix that?
turns.zh: 你不觉得让 LLM 给客户写东西会产生垃圾内容吗？就像 AI 垃圾？你怎么解决这个问题？

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, the CX team, our humans are the quality check on that, right? So we do not have AI send mass—like a lot of companies, other companies can do this and that's totally fine, no shame to other people. But a lot of other companies will say, hey, 100% of questions that come into our support team are going to be answered by an LLM first. And only if that customer writes back angrily will a human come in and be like, oh sorry about that, let me give you a real answer. And we just don't believe in that model. So I would much rather have AI draft an answer to the specific question based on the knowledge that it has coming in. And then a human can decide, is that a good answer or not. But very often it's like, gosh, this would have taken three sentences and instead I have three paragraphs of a reply that ultimately is not the most helpful. And we get so much feedback on support where people were like, was this AI because your response was so fast? And our team's really fast. So people think it's AI because it came to them so quickly. And then the second being like, wow, this is the first good interaction I've had with a support team in a long time. That's kind of sad for other tools and products out there. For us, it's one of the things that we give a lot of kudos to our team for, because it sets a brand impression, sometimes early in a customer's life cycle, and sometimes they've been with us for years and are writing in for the first time, and it gets them feeling confident they made the right decision. So I think you can use these tools. They're tools. I don't believe in blindly using these tools in a way that compromises your brand and ultimately makes your team feel like it's almost less useful or less knowledgeable because it's relying on a tool to have all the knowledge that a human should have.
turns.zh: 是的。我是说，客户体验团队——我们的人就是质量把关，对吧？所以我们不会让 AI 群发——很多公司、其他公司可以这么做，那完全没问题，对别人没有贬低之意。但很多其他公司会说，嘿，进入我们支持团队的问题 100% 都会先由 LLM 回答。只有当客户愤怒地回信时，才会有人类介入说，哦抱歉，让我给你一个真正的答案。我们就是不相信那种模式。所以我更愿意让 AI 根据它掌握的知识，针对具体问题起草一个答案。然后由人来判断，那是不是一个好答案。但很多时候情况是，天哪，这本来三句话就能说清，结果我得到三段回复，最终并不是最有帮助的。我们在支持方面收到很多反馈，人们会说，这是 AI 吗，因为你们回复得太快了？而我们团队真的很快。所以人们以为这是 AI，因为它来得太快了。然后第二类反馈是，哇，这是我很久以来和支持团队有过的最好互动。这对市面上其他工具和产品来说有点可悲。对我们来说，这是我们特别感谢团队的一点，因为它树立了品牌印象，有时是在客户生命周期的早期，有时他们和我们合作多年、第一次写信进来，这让他们对自己做了正确决定感到自信。所以我觉得你可以用这些工具。它们是工具。我不相信盲目使用这些工具，以至于损害你的品牌，最终让你的团队觉得自己几乎更没用、更没知识，因为它依赖一个工具来拥有本应由人掌握的全部知识。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: So you mentioned downsizing the customer experience team?
turns.zh: 所以你提到过缩减客户体验团队？

turns.en: Not downsizing, but I don't think we've ramped it in terms of headcount as we would have without it, right? So I think some of these tools are very helpful for enabling us to not always have to grow teams linearly with how fast the business is growing, right? And I think on other parts of the business, like marketing and other areas, where it's like, okay, we can do interviews with customers for customer stories, and we can have an AI tool transcribe this interview, pull out some of the most compelling pieces, but we still have a human write the story, right? So it's just deciding where you're going to use it. We don't like the way that a lot of AI writing feels. So we'll use it to help us find the interesting parts of two hours that we spent with a customer. But in a lot of ways, for it to feel like how we want Linear to feel, which is custom and handcrafted, we shouldn't use those tools for certain kinds of things.
turns.zh: 不是缩减，但我觉得如果没有这些工具，我们的员工人数会增长得更多。所以我认为其中一些工具非常有用，能让我们不必总是随着业务的增长速度线性地扩充团队。在业务的其他部分，比如市场营销和其他领域，我们可以为客户故事采访客户，用 AI 工具转录这段采访，提取出最精彩的部分，但故事仍然由人来写。所以关键在于决定在哪些地方使用它。我们不喜欢很多 AI 写作给人的感觉。所以我们会用它来帮我们找出与客户相处两小时中最有趣的部分。但在很多方面，为了让 Linear 保持我们想要的那种定制和手工打造的感觉，某些类型的事情我们不应该用那些工具。

turns.en: At least until they get better.
turns.zh: 至少等它们变得更好之前。

turns.en: Yeah. Faster is pretty good at writing, I've noticed recently. But anyway, how do sales engineers fit into your team, in the sales team?
turns.zh: 是啊。我最近注意到 Faster 在写作方面相当不错。不过话说回来，销售工程师在你的团队里、在销售团队里扮演什么角色？

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. So we have what we call Solutions Engineers, but effectively the same thing. They are kind of like partners to our enterprise account execs and probably the upper end of our growth segment. And so they're spending a lot of time with sales when a customer has really deep workflow questions, or they're thinking about, hey, I integrate with this tool over here with a very custom API integration. How would I move that to Linear? Right? So you're asking someone who has a deeper technical question, right? Or how would I perform a migration of 30,000 people from a legacy tool to Linear, right? And so a Solutions Engineer can come in with a technical mindset. All of these folks can build lots of—
turns.zh: 是的，是的。我们有所谓的解决方案工程师，但实际上是同一回事。他们有点像我们企业客户主管以及增长业务高端客户的合作伙伴。所以当客户有非常深入的工作流问题时，他们会花大量时间和销售一起工作，或者客户在想，嘿，我用一个非常定制的 API 集成接入了这个工具，我要怎么把它迁移到 Linear？对吧？所以你在问一个技术问题更深的人，对吧？或者我要怎么把 3 万人从一个遗留工具迁移到 Linear，对吧？所以解决方案工程师可以带着技术思维介入。这些人全都能搭建很多——

turns.en: To is an engineer presumably?
turns.zh: 那想必是工程师吧？

turns.en: Yes, almost always. And so that person has very detailed questions, and sometimes the people on our team are building full end-to-end demos of, oh, you wanted to see how we would integrate with ServiceNow? I actually built this ServiceNow integration overnight, let me show it to you. So it also makes a lot of these transitions that customers are going through very easy, because they start to see, wow, it is possible to do these things very quickly, and migrating isn't that hard, right? Because this engineer just built this quick importer in a day, right? So sometimes we're helping customers along in the journey. We're typically not going into their systems with access to their systems in a forward-deployed engineering type of way to implement Linear. And I think a lot of that is a philosophical belief: we believe Linear should be easy enough for someone to integrate. And we have competitors that have admins whose entire job is just managing that tool, and they are dedicated tool people within companies. And again, I think that works fine for products that are almost infinitely customizable, right? But Linear is not that. We tend to be far more of a purpose-built tool. So we have pretty clear ways of doing things within Linear, but I also think that makes things far easier for agents to understand, right? A lot of people are coming to Linear from other tools where, like, bug as a label for this one team means something and for another team means something else. And you can do that because a bunch of different teams can work in completely different ways, but it means that the data is very difficult to discern. And so we're finding that with our system it's just far easier for agents to read and understand and work with as a result of some of these things. So I think the combination of having that and then having a technical counterpart to a salesperson—and often our salespeople are working with people who are, you know, we have a champion in the company and they're saying, Linear is amazing, but I can't convince this other person. Can you help me? Right? The IT person or the procurement person or someone else who's often not in the tool day-to-day, right? So maybe doesn't understand the challenges. And our salespeople are basically advocates for that person and are like, okay, what can I do to help you sell internally? Right? And engineers are often not used to being like, I need to sell other people within my company about this tool, right? So that's a learned skill that we can often help with, and we find our salespeople are in interesting positions helping advocate for Linear through other people.
turns.zh: 是的，几乎总是。所以那个人有非常具体的问题，有时我们团队的人会搭建完整的端到端演示，比如，哦，你想看看我们如何与 ServiceNow 集成？我其实一夜之间就把这个 ServiceNow 集成搭好了，让我展示给你看。所以这也让客户正在经历的许多过渡变得非常容易，因为他们开始看到，哇，这些事情确实可以很快做到，迁移也没那么难，对吧？因为这个工程师一天之内就搭好了这个快速导入器，对吧？所以有时我们是在客户的旅程中帮助他们。我们通常不会以“前置部署工程师”的方式进入他们的系统、访问他们的系统来实施 Linear。我认为这在很大程度上是一种理念信念：我们相信 Linear 应该足够简单，让人能自己集成。我们有些竞争对手有管理员，他们的全部工作就是管理那个工具，公司里有专门负责该工具的人。再说一次，我认为这对几乎可以无限定制的产品来说没问题，对吧？但 Linear 不是那样。我们更像是一个专门用途的工具。所以我们在 Linear 内有相当清晰的操作方式，但我也认为这让智能体更容易理解，对吧？很多人从其他工具来到 Linear，在那里，“bug”这个标签对某个团队意味着一种东西，对另一个团队意味着另一种东西。你可以这样做，因为很多不同的团队可以以完全不同的方式工作，但这意味着数据非常难以辨别。所以我们发现，由于这些原因，我们的系统对智能体来说更容易读取、理解和操作。所以我认为，把这一点和给销售人员配一个技术搭档结合起来——而且我们的销售人员经常和这样的人合作：我们在公司里有一个拥护者，他们说，Linear 太棒了，但我无法说服另一个人。你能帮我吗？对吧？比如 IT 人员、采购人员，或者其他通常不日常使用这个工具的人，对吧？所以他们可能不理解这些挑战。我们的销售人员基本上就是那个人的倡导者，说，好的，我能做什么来帮你在内部推销？对吧？而工程师通常不习惯说，我需要向公司里的其他人推销这个工具，对吧？所以这是一种可以学习的技能，我们经常能帮上忙，我们发现我们的销售人员处于有趣的位置，通过其他人来为 Linear 做倡导。

turns.en: Just curious, how long does it—do you have a rule of thumb for how long it takes for a case like that, for you to get that customer to actually buy? Like when they have to go to, I don't know, someone who has decision-making authority.
turns.zh: 只是好奇，这要多久——对于这样的案例，你们有没有经验法则，从开始到让客户真正购买要多久？比如当他们必须去找，我不知道，有决策权的人。

turns.en: Like the champion, sorry.
turns.zh: 比如那个拥护者，抱歉。

turns.en: Yeah, sure. I mean, I think sometimes a decision can start from one person. We've seen this, and then they get the buy-in of the CEO and the CEO just makes a top-down decision and it's like removing a linear over the weekend—like get used to it or get out. And it's very dictatorial around the decision that's being made, and those decisions can happen in a month, right?
turns.zh: 是的，当然。我的意思是，我认为有时决策可以从一个人开始。我们见过这种情况，然后他们获得 CEO 的支持，CEO 直接自上而下做决定，就像周末把 Linear 移除——要么适应，要么走人。围绕正在做出的决定非常独断，而那些决定可以在一个月内发生，对吧？

turns.en: And those are like some other companies I'm assuming?
turns.zh: 我猜那些是其他一些公司？

turns.en: I mean, we had that happen at a 1,000-person company. So again, it's just like if you have a CEO who is like—you know, I'm less of that type of person. If I think my team should use a tool, I'll be like, why don't you all evaluate it and decide for yourselves, right? Other companies work in very different ways, right? So you have to think about the politics of a given organization, and every organization is inherently political in some shape or form. And then how do you ultimately work this decision into a favorable way for your business? But then we'll see—we had one company that probably took two years, two and a half years or something. And it wasn't that they were in the sales pipeline the whole time. It was like they came in, oh, we couldn't convince the CTO.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我们在一家 1000 人的公司遇到过这种情况。所以再说一次，如果你有一个那样的 CEO——你知道，我不是那种类型的人。如果我认为我的团队应该使用某个工具，我会说，你们为什么不评估一下，自己决定呢？对吧？其他公司的运作方式非常不同，对吧？所以你必须考虑特定组织的政治，每个组织在某种程度上本质上都是政治的。然后你最终如何把这个决定引导到对你的业务有利的方向？但然后我们会看到——我们有一家公司大概花了两年、两年半左右。并不是他们一直在销售管道里。而是他们来了，哦，我们无法说服 CTO。

turns.en: Like, and then they come in again like nine months later and start using it in the company.
turns.zh: 然后他们大概九个月后又来一次，开始在公司里用起来。

turns.en: Yeah, then a different person comes in like nine months later and it's like, I think we can convince the CTO now, right? And it just takes a really long time to finally get them to approve and make the decision. Sometimes it's budget. It's like, oh, we've already set the budget for this year, and if this is going to require more spend, well, that's going to be a 2028 decision, right? Some companies operate like that.
turns.zh: 对，然后九个月后换一个人来，说，我觉得现在可以说服 CTO 了，对吧？最后让他们批准并做出决定，真的要花很长时间。有时候是预算问题。比如，我们今年的预算已经定好了，如果这需要更多支出，那得等到 2028 年再决定，对吧？有些公司就是这么运作的。

turns.en: And so, are they now operating a lot faster because of the way things are changing so fast now, or not really, still?
turns.zh: 那么，因为现在变化太快，他们现在的运作速度快多了吗，还是其实并没有？

turns.en: Um, maybe like these more legacy companies?
turns.zh: 嗯，也许那些更传统的公司吧？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I don't think they're operating any faster, honestly, at least with decisions like this. I would say for a lot of these companies, the thing that's helping them move faster is that AI tools have effectively been unblocked, right? So if they believe that the engineering team in particular believes that this tool is going to make them better, and it fits in the AI budget for some companies — you know, that is maybe not infinite, but it is very high, whatever that budget is. And it was like add-on budget that kind of had to come out of nowhere, right? I think that's going to change.
turns.zh: 说实话，我不觉得他们的运作变快了，至少这类决策上没有。我想说，对很多这类公司来说，帮他们加快速度的是 AI 工具实际上被放行了，对吧？所以如果他们相信，尤其是工程团队相信这个工具能让他们变得更好，而且它能算进某些公司的 AI 预算里——你知道，那笔预算也许不是无限的，但非常高，不管具体是多少。而且那像是额外追加的预算，几乎是从天而降的，对吧？我觉得这会变。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Um, it's starting to change for companies, but in a lot of ways, if you can fit your company into that AI budget, then you are unlocking budget that previously didn't exist, right? And so that makes it far easier, I think, for companies to make a decision, because it's like, oh, there is budget. We've magically found budget that didn't previously exist, you know.
turns.zh: 嗯，对公司来说这开始变了，但很多时候，如果你能把自己塞进那笔 AI 预算里，你就是在释放以前不存在的预算，对吧？所以我觉得这让公司做决定容易得多，因为就像，哦，有预算。我们神奇地找到了以前不存在的预算。

turns.en: Okay, so you think a lot of these AI companies are getting to $100 million of revenue within like 3 months — that's because of this? Basically, it's like a lot of companies that previously didn't have budget for experimenting with new tools. They're just kind of like, oh my god, our company's going to die if we don't try any of these tools. So let's just experiment, and then at some point, maybe a year from now, 2 years from now, that's going to stop. Like they're experimenting right now, and then they're going to figure out what actually works, what doesn't.
turns.zh: 好，所以你觉得很多 AI 公司能在三个月内做到 1 亿美元营收，就是因为这个？基本上，就是很多公司以前没有预算去试验新工具。他们现在就像，天哪，如果我们不试试这些工具，公司就要完蛋了。那就先试试吧，然后到了某个时候，也许一年后、两年后，这就会停下来。他们现在在试验，然后会搞清楚什么真正有用、什么没用。

turns.en: I think a lot of companies are experimenting, and you're signing like 1-year deals maybe with companies, or you're signing pilot agreements with companies that have costs associated with them still, um, but you're not signing a 3-year deal with a company because you're like, I don't know if I'm going to like this in 2 years. Like things are changing so rapidly, right?
turns.zh: 我觉得很多公司在试验，你可能会跟公司签一年期的合同，或者签试点协议，这些仍然有相关成本，嗯，但你不会跟一家公司签三年期的合同，因为你会想，我不知道两年后我还会不会喜欢这个。事情变化太快了，对吧？

turns.en: Is it normal for a company to sign a 3-year deal?
turns.zh: 公司签三年期合同正常吗？

turns.en: Um, if you're trusted, like we sometimes sign very long-term deals for that reason. It has trade-offs, right? Like we can't move up our prices in that 3-year period of time unless you have step-ups built in to the agreement, but you know that you have that committed revenue, right? So, and for the business the same is true. They feel like maybe they're getting a discount for three years that they wouldn't have otherwise been getting.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果你值得信任的话，我们有时候确实会因此签很长期的合同。这有取舍，对吧？比如在那三年里我们不能涨价，除非协议里内置了阶梯涨价条款，但你知道你有那笔承诺收入，对吧？对企业来说也一样。他们觉得自己也许拿到了三年折扣，否则是拿不到的。

turns.en: But to the example you had, I mean, I think a lot of those businesses are very concentrated in the customers that they have, right? So it's very different, I think, to be a business like Linear that is, you know, 40,000 paying customers, right? And historically up until June was an entirely seat-based business, right? Um, much harder to grow revenue from zero to 100 million overnight, right?
turns.zh: 但就你举的例子来说，我觉得很多这类企业的客户非常集中，对吧？所以我觉得，做像 Linear 这样的企业很不一样——你知道，我们有 4 万个付费客户，对吧？而且历史上一直到六月，我们完全是按席位收费的业务，对吧？嗯，要把营收一夜之间从零做到 1 亿美元，那难得多，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Um, and then you see companies where, I don't know, you sell to the defense industry or you sell to gigantic law firms or something like that. And you sign a few deals that are like 30 to $40 million in ARR, and then okay great, we got to 100 million in ARR, right? So certain kinds of businesses do have more of that profile.
turns.zh: 嗯，然后你会看到有些公司，比如，卖给国防行业，或者卖给巨型律所之类的。你签几笔 3000 万到 4000 万美元 ARR 的单子，然后好极了，我们就做到 1 亿美元 ARR 了，对吧？所以某些类型的企业确实更符合那种画像。

turns.en: So, you're usage-based now?
turns.zh: 所以你们现在是按用量收费了？

turns.en: Uh, we have some features that are usage-based in terms of how we charge for them, yeah.
turns.zh: 呃，我们有些功能在收费方式上是按用量计费的，对。

turns.en: So, how do you convince your customers that that's a good idea, to go from seat-based to usage-based? Was that hard to convince them?
turns.zh: 那你怎么说服客户，让他们觉得从按席位收费转向按用量收费是个好主意？说服他们难吗？

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I would say a lot of companies that are in the SaaS world are certainly moving to usage-based pricing. I think everyone would love for there to be almost like the Intercom Fin model that existed for a long period of time, which was like, oh, if AI responds to your support ticket, that costs a dollar. And you're like, is every support ticket that gets replied to worth a dollar?
turns.zh: 难。我是说，SaaS 世界里很多公司确实在转向按用量定价。我觉得大家都希望有那种几乎像 Intercom Fin 的模式——它存在了很长时间——就是，哦，如果 AI 回复了你的支持工单，那收一美元。然后你会想，每一张被回复的支持工单都值一美元吗？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Like, okay great. So you're pricing on the outcome that you drive, right? I think it's a lot harder for other types of businesses to be like, okay, so what is automatically triaging this bug to the right team worth?
turns.zh: 就像，好吧，很好。所以你是在按你带来的结果定价，对吧？我觉得对其他类型的企业来说，要回答“自动把这个 bug 分派给正确的团队值多少钱”就难得多。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Right? Maybe to every company, that's a little different. Maybe you believe, oh, that's the PM's job. Like they should be triaging bugs into the right queue, to the right person, right? Um, and maybe another company says, well, I'd want my PM to spend their time talking to customers and building the product roadmap and doing other things instead. So I think there can sometimes be a debate, in functions that are not very clearly outcome oriented, about how you charge for usage-based pricing.
turns.zh: 对吧？也许对每家公司来说都不太一样。也许你认为，哦，那是 PM 的活。他们就应该把 bug 分派到正确的队列、给正确的人，对吧？嗯，也许另一家公司说，我更希望我的 PM 把时间花在和客户交流、做产品路线图和别的事情上。所以我觉得，在那些结果导向不明显的职能里，怎么按用量定价有时会有争论。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Um, so I would love for there to be a world where there is some kind of outcome-based model that makes sense for our world. I don't know that there is. So for now we're mostly charging based off of the costs that we incur to run our services.
turns.zh: 嗯，所以我希望存在一个世界，里面有某种适合我们这种业务的、基于结果的模式。我不确定有没有。所以目前我们主要根据运行服务所产生的成本来收费。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Um, and in some cases those costs can be pretty high.
turns.zh: 嗯，在某些情况下那些成本可能相当高。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Um, if you're running a coding session in Linear, or if you're doing things like, run through my entire backlog and tell me what I should work on next — you know, you could have a very large backlog of a lot of things, right? So those kinds of even just chat questions to the agent can be more expensive. We've decided to make certain things free. So, like, Linear agent chat conversations are free, and we think we can continue to drive down the costs for that over time.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果你在 Linear 里跑一个编码会话，或者你做那种“把我整个待办列表过一遍，告诉我接下来该做什么”的事——你知道，你可能有一个非常大的待办列表，对吧？所以这类东西，哪怕只是向智能体提的聊天问题，都可能更贵。我们决定把某些东西做成免费的。比如，Linear 智能体的聊天对话是免费的，我们认为可以随着时间推移继续降低这方面的成本。

turns.en: Are you guys using open source models for that?
turns.zh: 你们那方面用的是开源模型吗？

turns.en: Right now we're using Frontier.
turns.zh: 目前我们用的是前沿模型。

turns.en: Okay. Even for the chat?
turns.zh: 好。连聊天也是？

turns.en: Even for the chat. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 连聊天也是。对，对，对。

turns.en: And, you know, TBD with the fusion holds there. And then beyond that, when you have a coding session in Linear, you can choose between, right now, OpenAI or Anthropic models and harnesses, and the user ultimately gets to decide there. And we charge basically by saying, here's what we were charged from the API, here's the published rate, and we charge a little bit on top of that. And that's it. So making it very clear and transparent for most users. And then for products like Loops, we have an AI credits model as well for that feature. So for everything else, it's a little different. The vast majority of our AI features are just baked into Linear and you don't have to pay extra for them.
turns.zh: 而且，那个 fusion holds 的部分还有待确定。再往后，当你在 Linear 里进行一次编码会话时，你可以在 OpenAI 或 Anthropic 的模型和 harness 之间选择，最终由用户决定。我们的收费方式基本上是：这是我们被 API 收取的费用，这是公开的费率，我们在此基础上加一点点。就这样。所以对大多数用户来说，这非常清晰透明。而对于像 Loops 这样的产品，我们针对那个功能也有 AI credits 模式。所以其他东西就有点不一样。我们绝大多数的 AI 功能都直接内置在 Linear 里，你不需要额外付费。

turns.en: How do you go about going to your customer and saying, hey, previously you guys were doing seat-based pricing and now we're going to do this?
turns.zh: 你是怎么去跟客户说，嘿，你们之前是按席位收费，现在我们要改成这样？

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think it helps that the seat-based pricing isn't going away, right? So you're still paying for the core service, and we are not charging for things that were previously otherwise free.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得有帮助的一点是，按席位收费并没有消失，对吧？所以你仍然在为核心服务付费，我们也没有对以前免费的东西开始收费。

turns.en: Oh, I see.
turns.zh: 哦，我明白了。

turns.en: So it's very different, I think, when you go to a customer and you're like, yeah, so what was free is now paid and usage-based.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，如果你跑去跟客户说“对，以前免费的东西现在要收费了，而且是按用量计费”，那情况就完全不一样了。

turns.en: So these are like new features basically.
turns.zh: 所以这些基本上都是新功能。

turns.en: Exactly. So sometimes we'll have a feature that's in a beta period and we don't exactly know what it's going to cost or how to charge for it with usage-based pricing, because, you know, you can, for example, run a very expensive Linear agent query and you can run a very inexpensive one, right? So charging based purely off of, you know, $1 per query wouldn't make sense in that world, right? So sometimes you just need to let customers play with a new product to determine what it's going to cost and what the best pricing model is. So typically what we'll do is we'll have a feature that's in beta and we'll say, hey, this is an AI feature in beta, we expect that we will charge for this in the future, but right now it's free.
turns.zh: 没错。所以有时候我们会有一个处于 beta 期的功能，我们并不确切知道它的成本是多少，也不知道该怎么按用量计费，因为比如你可以跑一个非常昂贵的 Linear 智能体查询，也可以跑一个非常便宜的，对吧？所以纯粹按每次查询 1 美元来收费，在那个情况下就不合理，对吧？所以有时候你只需要让客户去试用一个新产品，来确定它的成本是多少、最佳的定价模式是什么。所以我们通常的做法是，有一个处于 beta 期的功能，然后我们会说，嘿，这是一个 beta 期的 AI 功能，我们预计未来会对它收费，但现在它是免费的。

turns.en: Mhm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Feel free to use it, see if you get value out of it, give us feedback, and then when we're ready to charge for it, we will let you know and give you notice. And I think that's worked generally pretty well for us so far. And you know, just trying to make sure that we're very clear with our customers. Sometimes, you know, we can have a six-month beta period and then five months later you're like, oh, I totally forgot that this was free and in beta and now I'm going to be charged for it and I'm disappointed, right? It's hard, you know, there's nothing we could have done other than, I don't know, warning banners in our product like “you are using a free feature that will soon be paid.” So there's only so much you can do about that, but I think just trying to be open and honest with your customers that we don't know what the business model is for this. We know we're going to charge for it because it's expensive, it's an expensive product to serve to you. But we are going to try and be as transparent as possible and we hope you trust us, right? And hopefully every time one of these things happens you are building more trust over time. I'll also say we tend to bias towards making things more expensive at the start and then decreasing costs, rather than making things really cheap and then being like, oops, actually we can't serve this product for that cheap, right? So just being conservative in that way, and where we are able to lower costs for customers so that we get more adoption, we will.

turns.en: Maybe one example: I think Stripe did so well as a company that in a lot of ways, when you're a 140-160 billion dollar company and you're on that rise, sometimes you believe you can always hire better than what you have today. So you have a leader in a given function that's doing well. And sometimes your first reaction to that could be like, well, it's because the business is doing well, not because that person necessarily is that great.
turns.zh: 也许一个例子：我认为 Stripe 作为一家公司做得太好了，以至于在很多方面，当你是一家市值 1400 到 1600 亿美元的公司，并且处于上升期时，你有时会相信自己总能招到比现有更好的人。所以你在某个职能上有一位表现很好的领导者。有时你的第一反应可能是：嗯，那是因为业务做得好，而不是因为那个人一定那么出色。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And if like, oh, I'm at Google. I helped increase revenue by, you know, 20 billion dollars. But like what did you really do, right? Um and so sometimes it goes really well. Is it, you know, because of that person or is it because the business was going really well? And then if the company is doing so well that you can attract really high quality talent, right? So someone like two levels above that person and then a year later you're able to attract a person who's two levels above that person and, right? You're kind of always going to be seeking like someone better than who you haven't seen because you can. And I think like for a lot of companies, like being able to say like like I've said this to our founders, I'm like we can get someone better. Like we're a good company, company that people want to work for and then are excited about. Like we don't have to settle, right? And I think that's like great. And then at the same time, sometimes you also have to like really recognize like the great people that you have. And I think for Stripe it took a longer time to like come around to that. Like Stripe's been having a lot of like boomerangs. Like, you know, people left the company because maybe they, you know, weren't on the rise, you know, in the way that they wanted to be and then, you know, came back and are doing like amazingly well. And I think sometimes I would like to look back on my time at Linear and say like the right people were like promoted and excelled and we didn't hire about them unless the company needed to, right? Unless we needed to get to that a different stage, we needed something that that person didn't have and not just because like we weren't willing to let them try to like be better than they are, to like scale at that next stage because you know, in running startups, this is true of founders like you don't like almost no founder who has a lot of success has like done it exactly before, right? And that's probably going to be true of a lot of the early team like they're leaders at the company, but they've never scaled a support team to like 200 people or 500 people or whatever. That doesn't mean that they can't, right? Just like it doesn't mean that that founder can't be a great founder at 1,000 people and also a great founder at like 50 people. And so like I just fundamentally believe that like people can grow and scale and that you should like reward that over time and you know, I've sometime like different parts of of the company like I'm like I don't know if they always believe that. I think and I think a lot has changed since then for what it's worth, but maybe that's one thing.
turns.zh: 然后如果有人说，哦，我在谷歌，我帮助增加了 200 亿美元的收入。但你到底做了什么？所以有时事情进展顺利。是因为那个人，还是因为业务本身发展得很好？然后，如果公司发展得如此之好，以至于你能吸引到非常高质量的人才，对吧？比如比那个人高两级的人，一年后你又能吸引到比那个人高两级的人，对吧？你总是会寻找比你没见过的人更好的人，因为你能做到。我认为对很多公司来说，能够说——就像我对我们的创始人说过的那样——我们可以找到更好的人。我们是一家好公司，是人们想要为之工作并感到兴奋的公司。我们不必将就，对吧？我认为这很棒。但同时，有时你也必须真正认识到你所拥有的优秀人才。我认为 Stripe 花了更长时间才意识到这一点。Stripe 有很多回旋镖式员工。比如，人们离开公司，也许是因为他们没有以自己想要的方式上升，然后他们回来了，做得非常出色。有时我会回顾我在 Linear 的时光，说正确的人得到了晋升和发挥，我们没有在他们之上招聘，除非公司需要，对吧？除非我们需要进入不同的阶段，我们需要那个人没有的东西，而不是因为我們不愿意让他们尝试变得更好，在下一个阶段扩大规模，因为你知道，在经营初创公司时，这对创始人来说也是如此——几乎没有一个取得巨大成功的创始人之前做过完全相同的事情，对吧？这很可能也适用于许多早期团队，他们是公司的领导者，但他们从未将支持团队扩展到 200 人或 500 人左右。这并不意味着他们不能，对吧？就像这并不意味着那个创始人不能在 1000 人时成为伟大的创始人，也不能在 50 人时成为伟大的创始人。所以我从根本上相信人们可以成长和扩展，你应该随着时间的推移奖励这一点，你知道，我有时觉得公司的不同部门——我不确定他们是否总是相信这一点。我认为，而且我认为从那时起已经发生了很多变化，但也许这是一个方面。

turns.en: On support, that would be the other thing. They know lots of great people at great companies and can introduce you to people who are more knowledgeable than they are in certain areas. So often investors will come to me and be like, "Can you help this founder who's thinking about building a sales team from zero?" turns.en: Yeah yeah yeah yeah. And we work with some great investors and they're very helpful and have referred people, but in a lot of situations, closed mouths don't get fed. So if you don't ask for things, they're not going to give them to you.
turns.zh: 对对对对。我们跟一些很优秀的投资人合作，他们非常帮忙，也给我们引荐过人，但很多时候，闭着的嘴吃不到饭。所以如果你不开口要，他们不会主动给你。

turns.en: So Linear doesn't have any other C-suite other than the founders and you?
turns.zh: 所以 Linear 除了几位创始人和你之外，没有别的 C 级高管？

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Why is that?
turns.zh: 为什么会这样？

turns.en: It's a good question. I mean, I think again, we operated this way at Stripe for a very long time. So again, I have a bias towards it, but I think it's been true actually for a lot of companies. You might have one executive who's hired in on the business side who has this title or something similar. And I would say at the beginning a lot of it is just, my role is kind of a catch-all for a really small company for lots of different functions and things over time. But I expect that to change. I don't think that's going to be the way it is forever. If we build out the right team, the right leadership in the right places, people will earn that level of title. And I think for us right now, because we still feel so small, we're about 170 people, in a lot of ways we want to remain pretty flat rather than adding a lot of layers when we are still pretty small. And I think that's been helpful for us so far. But that doesn't mean that we haven't promoted people and given people more responsibility, more ownership, more scope. But we tend to focus on things like head-of titles for wide areas of ownership.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题。我觉得，我们在 Stripe 很长一段时间也是这么运作的。所以我对这种方式有偏好，但我觉得实际上很多公司都是这样。你可能只在业务侧招了一位高管，给他这个头衔或者类似的东西。我想说，一开始很大程度上是因为，在一个很小的公司里，我的角色有点像各种职能的兜底，随着时间推移什么都管一点。但我预计这会改变。我不认为会永远这样。如果我们把合适的团队搭起来，在合适的位置放上合适的领导，人们会凭本事赢得那个级别的头衔。我觉得对我们来说，现在因为我们还觉得自己很小，大概 170 人，很多方面我们想保持相当扁平，而不是在还很小的时候就加很多层级。我觉得到目前为止这对我们很有帮助。但这不代表我们没有提拔过人、没有给人更多责任、更多主导权、更大的职责范围。只是我们倾向于聚焦在“负责人”这类头衔上，对应的是很宽的职责范围。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, I mean, that's all I had. Is there anything else that you wanted to talk about?
turns.zh: 对。对，我想问的就这些了。你还有什么想聊的吗？

turns.en: No, no. This was a great conversation. I feel like we went into a lot of different areas of a business. So thanks. You had great questions.
turns.zh: 没有没有。这是一次很棒的对话。我觉得我们聊到了企业的很多不同方面。谢谢，你的问题很好。

turns.en: Yeah, thank you.
turns.zh: 好，谢谢你。

consensus.en: Issue tracking is dead; the future is agentic product development systems.
consensus.zh: 问题追踪已死；未来是智能体式产品开发系统。

consensus.en: Agents now create over 50% of issues on Linear, changing work creation fundamentally.
consensus.zh: 智能体现在创建了 Linear 上超过 50% 的问题，从根本上改变了工作的创建方式。

consensus.en: Companies should bring agentic workflows into their tools, not just expose data via MCP.
consensus.zh: 公司应将智能体式工作流引入自己的工具，而不仅仅是通过 MCP 暴露数据。

consensus.en: Hiring should be deliberate with work trials; scaling teams linearly is outdated.
consensus.zh: 招聘应通过工作试用期审慎进行；线性扩展团队已过时。

consensus.en: AI tools should augment, not replace, human quality checks in support and content.
consensus.zh: AI 工具应增强而非取代人类在支持和内容方面的质量检查。

consensus.en: Speed and adaptability now matter more than long-term planning in AI-driven markets.
consensus.zh: 在 AI 驱动的市场中，速度和适应性现在比长期规划更重要。

contrarian.en: Being a database with an MCP server is not a great business model; you must own the UX.
contrarian.zh: 做一个带 MCP 服务器的数据库不是好的商业模式；你必须拥有用户体验。

contrarian.en: Don't blindly let LLMs answer all support queries; humans must draft and review.
contrarian.zh: 不要盲目让 LLM 回答所有支持查询；必须由人类起草和审核。

contrarian.en: Not every company needs a COO; hire functional leaders only when you know what great looks like.
contrarian.zh: 不是每家公司都需要 COO；只有当你清楚“优秀”的标准时，才招聘职能领导者。

contrarian.en: Avoid hiring SDRs; AEs should do outbound with tooling, not waste customer time.
contrarian.zh: 避免招聘 SDR；AE 应利用工具进行外呼，而不是浪费客户时间。

contrarian.en: Usage-based pricing is hard for non-outcome functions; charge based on costs incurred.
contrarian.zh: 对于非结果导向的职能，基于使用量的定价很难；应根据产生的成本收费。

contrarian.en: Don't always hire over your leaders; reward and grow the great people you have.
contrarian.zh: 不要总是空降比现有领导者更强的人；奖励并培养你拥有的优秀人才。
